* For the convergent-function reading of FAE / hindsight bias / self-serving bias / autobiographical reconstruction as facets of one editorial process: there is no single source that takes this position; the synthesis is the book's own. The component biases each have extensive literatures of their own.


### Chapter 4 — Pronin and the Bias Blind Spot

* Pronin, Emily, Lin, Daniel Y., and Ross, Lee (2002), "The bias blind spot: Perceptions of bias in self versus others," _Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin_ , 28(3), 369–381. The original empirical paper. Effect size d ≈ 0.3–0.5, as cited in the Coda.
* Pronin, Emily (2007), "Perception and misperception of bias in human judgment," _Trends in Cognitive Sciences_ , 11(1), 37–43. The accessible review.


### Chapter 5 — Confirmation Bias and the Wason Task

* Wason, P. C. (1968), "Reasoning about a rule," _Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology_ , 20(3), 273–281. The original selection-task paper.
* Nickerson, Raymond S. (1998), "Confirmation bias: A ubiquitous phenomenon in many guises," _Review of General Psychology_ , 2(2), 175–220. The standard comprehensive review.
* For the algorithmic-feed amplification discussion: see the broader literature on recommender systems and engagement optimization (Zuboff, Tufekci, Vaidhyanathan have written extensively for general readers).


### Chapter 6 — Kahan and the Smart-People Problem

* Kahan, Dan M., Peters, Ellen, Dawson, Erica Cantrell, and Slovic, Paul (2017), "Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government," _Behavioural Public Policy_ , 1(1), 54–86. The motivated-numeracy paper. The Coda notes that the magnitudes vary across replications.
* Kahan, Dan M. (2013), "Ideology, motivated reasoning, and cognitive reflection," _Judgment and Decision Making_ , 8(4), 407–424. An earlier paper introducing identity-protective cognition.
* For the historical Coughlin/Long material in §6.4: Brinkley, Alan. _Voices of Protest: Huey Long, Father Coughlin, and the Great Depression_ (1982), New York: Knopf, is the standard scholarly treatment of both figures.

blocks.en_title: Further Reading
blocks.src:
### Chapter 7 — Tribal Truth

* Haidt, Jonathan. _The Righteous Mind_ (2012), New York: Pantheon. The accessible treatment of moral and political tribal cognition.
* Mason, Lilliana. _Uncivil Agreement: How Politics Became Our Identity_ (2018), Chicago: University of Chicago Press. The empirical case for tribal identity as the load-bearing variable in modern American political belief.
* Greene, Joshua. _Moral Tribes_ (2013), New York: Penguin. The complementary cognitive-science perspective.


### Chapter 8 — The Limits of Awareness and Effort

* For the empirical evidence on awareness-doesn't-cure-bias: there is no single canonical citation; the finding is replicated across many specific biases. Reviews include Lilienfeld, S. O., Ammirati, R., and Landfield, K. (2009), "Giving debiasing away: Can psychological research on correcting cognitive errors promote human welfare?" _Perspectives on Psychological Science_ , 4(4), 390–398.
* For the rationalist-trap material: there is no single source that names the trap as Chapter 8 names it; the synthesis is the book's own, drawing on the broader sociological and self-critical literature within the rationalist and EA communities. The 2023 _Time_ magazine investigation by Charlotte Alter and the EA Forum's post-FTX discussions are the primary public sources for the FTX-EA case discussed in §8.7.
* For Pinto et al. 2017 on split-brain findings (referenced in §8.4 and the Coda): see Chapter 1 citations.


### Chapter 9 — Mercier and Sperber

* Mercier, Hugo, and Sperber, Dan. _The Enigma of Reason_ (2017), Cambridge: Harvard University Press. The book-length development of the argumentative theory.
* Mercier, Hugo, and Sperber, Dan (2011), "Why do humans reason? Arguments for an argumentative theory," _Behavioral and Brain Sciences_ , 34(2), 57–74. The original peer-review article with extensive responses, both supporting and critical.
* For the contested status of the argumentative theory: see the open peer commentary published with the 2011 paper, particularly responses from dual-process theorists. Stanovich, Keith E. _The Robot's Rebellion_ (2004) and _Rationality and the Reflective Mind_ (2011) develop the alternative position.
* Galef, Julia. _The Scout Mindset_ (2021), New York: Portfolio. The complementary disposition-focused framework discussed in §9.3.


### Chapter 10 — Structural Tools

* Tetlock, Philip E., and Gardner, Dan. _Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction_ (2015), New York: Crown. The accessible synthesis of the Good Judgment Project. The Coda notes that superforecasters are the top ~2% of self-selected participants.
* Tetlock, Philip E. _Expert Political Judgment_ (2005), Princeton: Princeton University Press. The original empirical work.
* Klein, Gary (2007), "Performing a project pre-mortem," _Harvard Business Review_ , September issue. The pre-mortem technique as Klein originally framed it.
* Sunstein, Cass R., and Hastie, Reid. _Wiser: Getting Beyond Groupthink to Make Groups Smarter_ (2014), Boston: Harvard Business Review Press. Practical structural tools for group-level decision-making.

blocks.en_title: Further Reading
blocks.src:
### Chapter 11 — Epistemic Friends and Institutional Tools

* For the four-conditions framing of epistemic friendship in §11.1: there is no single canonical source; the synthesis is the book's own, drawing on the broader friendship literature (Aristotle, Cicero, more recent work in social psychology) and on practical writing about adversarial collaboration.
* Mellers, Barbara A., and Tetlock, Philip E. (2019), "From discoveries to decisions: Explaining and improving societal predictions," American Behavioral Scientist. Adversarial-collaboration practices.
* For forecasting communities: Metaculus, Manifold, Good Judgment Open (mentioned in §11.3) all maintain public documentation and academic-paper bibliographies on their sites.


### Chapter 12 — The Practice and the Endpoints

* For the AI / LLM material in §12.3a: the discussion synthesizes published work on language-model sycophancy (Sharma, M. et al., 2023, "Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models," arXiv:2310.13548), AI companion effects on user cognition (the academic literature on this is rapidly evolving; Maples, B. et al., 2024, on Replika and emotional support, is one starting point), and the practical experience of AI-saturated cognition. Readers engaging this seriously should treat published work in this area as current rather than settled.
* For the political-endpoint material in §12.3 on the design of information environments: Zuboff, Shoshana. _The Age of Surveillance Capitalism_ (2019); Tufekci, Zeynep. _Twitter and Tear Gas_ (2017); Vaidhyanathan, Siva. _Antisocial Media_ (2018).


### Coda — Limits of the Framework

* For collective and mass-scale self-deception (referenced in the Coda): Arendt, Hannah. _The Origins of Totalitarianism_ (1951); Cohen, Stanley. _States of Denial: Knowing about Atrocities and Suffering_ (2001); Halbwachs, Maurice. _On Collective Memory_ (1992 English translation).
* For the protective-self-deception literature: Taylor, Shelley E. _Positive Illusions: Creative Self-Deception and the Healthy Mind_ (1989), New York: Basic Books. The classic counterweight to the structural-honesty framework.
* For cross-cultural cognition (referenced in the Coda's cultural-specificity section): Henrich, Joseph. _The WEIRDest People in the World_ (2020), New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, on the cultural specificity of much cognitive-science research.


### A Note on What This List Is Not

This is a working bibliography for readers who want to engage the load-bearing literature directly. It is not a comprehensive scholarly apparatus; the book is a synthesis written for general readers, not a scholarly monograph, and full academic citation throughout the body of the text would have changed the book's character. Readers planning to use this book in academic settings — citing its arguments, building on its framework, or critiquing its claims — should treat the body text as a starting point and the primary literature cited here as the load-bearing record.
